links.outcome: Hallucination rates and physician-rated response quality with versus without RAG
links.effect: Hallucination rates were 5/52, 10% with RAG versus 15/39, 38% with native ChatGPT (P=.002). RAG improved all evaluated response-quality dimensions (all P<.01).
links.quote: The ChatGPT+RAG model outperformed the native ChatGPT model across all evaluated response quality dimensions (all P<.01) and exhibited a significantly lower hallucination rate (5/52, 10% versus 15/39, 38%; P=.002).

links.outcome: Physician identification and correction of incorrect AI responses before consent completion
links.effect: Physicians reportedly identified all hallucinated or incorrect responses and corrected them at time point 5 before consent concluded. Independent detection sensitivity was not quantified.
links.quote: All hallucinated or incorrect responses were identified by the experienced physicians who were present throughout the informed consent consultations.

links.outcome: Patient satisfaction with physician-supervised AI-assisted informed consent
links.effect: Satisfaction remained high across groups. After chatbot interaction, RAG improved information-delivery satisfaction (P =.014) and perceived informedness (P =.007); native ChatGPT showed no significant changes (P =.28 and P =.06, respectively).
links.quote: By comparing traditional physician-led consultations with those assisted by ChatGPT and ChatGPT+RAG, we found that patient satisfaction remained consistently high across all groups, suggesting that the use of AI support did not compromise the informed consent experience.
